passages.text: Hearing loss associated with CDC42 in mice and humans (Takenouchi-Kosaki syndrome): CDC42 and RHOQ synergistically function in cochlear hair cells

CDC42 is involved in multiple signaling pathways, including actin organization and polarity. <sentence_start/>We previously reported progressive sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) in inner ear hair cell (HC)-specific <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-knockout (<italic toggle="yes">At</italic><italic toggle="yes">oh</italic><italic toggle="yes">1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>) mice. <sentence_start/>However, the phenotype was milder than expected, suggesting possible redundancy with other Rho-family GTPases. <sentence_start/>Thereafter, Takenouchi-Kosaki syndrome (TKS), caused by <italic toggle="yes">de novo CDC42</italic> mutations and manifesting as SNHL, was reported, in which the p.Y64C mutation was speculated to be constitutively active. <sentence_start/>However, the relationship between CDC42 status and hearing phenotypes in TKS remains unclear. <sentence_start/>Using cell models, mouse models, and patient data, we propose that impaired and/or dysregulated cycling between GDP/inactive and GTP/active forms, through either loss-of-function or constitutive activation, can lead to SNHL. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, to test redundancy, we generated HC-specific <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> double-knockout (<italic toggle="yes">At</italic><italic toggle="yes">oh</italic><italic toggle="yes">1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>) mice, which revealed synergistic roles of CDC42 and RHOQ in cochlear HCs. <sentence_start/>Supporting this synergy, MDCK cells with CDC42 and RHOQ double knockdown showed greater phospho-cofilin, a key regulator of actin turnover, elevation than single knockdowns.

Cell division cycle 42 (CDC42) is a member of the Rho family of small GTPases and is involved in multiple signaling pathways, including cytoskeleton organization and establishment of cell polarity at cellular and tissue levels (<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21115489" doi="10.1074/jbc.R110.200329" pmcid="PMC3024731" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30696065" doi="10.3390/cells8020092" pmcid="PMC6406560" count="1">2</citation>). <sentence_start/>Its function depends on tightly regulated cycling between GDP-bound inactive and GTP-bound active states, occurring in precise spatiotemporal contexts (<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21115489" doi="10.1074/jbc.R110.200329" pmcid="PMC3024731" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30696065" doi="10.3390/cells8020092" pmcid="PMC6406560" count="1">2</citation>), which is essential for the development and maintenance of actin-based structures. <sentence_start/>This regulation is controlled by three factors: guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs), and guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors (GDIs) (<citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30696065" doi="10.3390/cells8020092" pmcid="PMC6406560" count="1">2</citation>, <citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23918979" doi="10.4049/jimmunol.1300209" count="1">3</citation>). <sentence_start/>Recently, we showed that CDC42 is required for cochlear hair cell (HC) maintenance in inner ear HC-specific <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-knockout mice (<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO, <italic toggle="yes">At</italic><italic toggle="yes">oh</italic><italic toggle="yes">1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>) (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although morphological development was normal at postnatal day 8 (P8), <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice developed progressive sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) because of HC loss accompanied by abnormalities in stereocilia and apical junctional complexes (AJCs) (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>We also found that active CDC42 is localized to stereocilia and AJCs in cochlear HCs (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the hearing phenotype was milder than expected, suggesting functional redundancy with other CDC42-related GTPases, including Ras homolog family member Q (RHOQ, also referred to as TC10) and/or Ras homolog family member J (RHOJ), which belong to the same subgroup of Rho-family small GTPases as CDC42, although they were not investigated. <sentence_start/>In a cell-type-specific RNA-sequence study (<citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25904789" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.5126-14.2015" pmcid="PMC4405555" count="1">5</citation>), <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> mRNA was almost equally expressed in HCs and non-HCs in the developing inner ear (embryonic day 16 [E16]-P7); in sharp contrast, <italic toggle="yes">RhoJ</italic> mRNA was almost exclusively expressed in non-HCs. <sentence_start/>However, <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> mRNA expression levels in cochlear HCs are approximately one-quarter to one-fifth of those of <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> mRNA (<citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25904789" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.5126-14.2015" pmcid="PMC4405555" count="1">5</citation>), making its compensatory contribution uncertain.

After the report of HC-specific <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>), Takenouchi-Kosaki syndrome (TKS), which is caused by <italic toggle="yes">de novo</italic> mutations in <italic toggle="yes">CDC42</italic> and characterized by various brain anomalies, dysmorphic craniofacial features, hematological anomalies including macrothrombocytopenia and immunological dysfunction with recurrent infection, hypothyroidism, and SNHL, was reported. <sentence_start/>The first two patients carried the p.Y64C mutation (<citation rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26386261" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.37275" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26708094" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.37526" count="1">7</citation>). <sentence_start/>Subsequently, Martinelli <italic toggle="yes">et al.</italic> reported 15 patients with nine different <italic toggle="yes">CDC42</italic> mutations and classified TKS into three groups according to the mutants’ structure and function (<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29394990" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.12.015" pmcid="PMC5985417" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>Group I (original/typical TKS) mutants (Y64C, R66G, and R68Q) are located in the switch II region of CDC42 (amino acid [aa] 62 to 68 (<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11889037" doi="10.1093/emboj/21.6.1315" pmcid="PMC125919" count="1">9</citation>, <citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33347888" doi="10.1016/j.bpj.2020.12.007" pmcid="PMC7840443" count="1">10</citation>)), which mediates CDC42 binding to effectors and regulators. <sentence_start/>Group II mutants (C81F/Y, S83P, and A159V) lie within or near the nucleotide-binding pocket. <sentence_start/>Finally, Group III mutants (I21T, Y23C, and E171K) affect interactions with effectors containing CDC42/RAC-interacting binding (CRIB) motif (<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29394990" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.12.015" pmcid="PMC5985417" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>Two alternatively spliced CDC42 isoforms with distinct C-terminal regions (aa 163-191; a marked difference is <sup>182</sup>PKKSRRCVLL<sup>191</sup>X in isoform 1 and <sup>182</sup>TQPKRKCCIF<sup>191</sup>X in isoform 2) (<citation rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8954774" doi="10.1006/geno.1996.0586" count="1">11</citation>), exist in humans and mice; isoform 1 (exons 1-5 and 7) is ubiquitously expressed, while isoform 2 (exons 1-6) is predominantly expressed in the brain (<citation rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24059268" doi="10.1042/BJ20130788" count="1">12</citation>, <citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31601675" doi="10.1084/jem.20190147" pmcid="PMC6888978" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="bib14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.202004092" pmcid="PMC10883850" pmid="38386112" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>Mutations affecting only the C-terminus of isoform 1 spare the intact brain-dominant isoform 2, leading to weakened actinopathies, including no SNHL (<citation rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32424669" doi="10.1007/s10875-020-00786-7" count="1">15</citation>). <sentence_start/>Indeed, nine patients with <italic toggle="yes">CDC42</italic> mutations in the C-terminus of isoform 1 (R186C, C188Y, and X192CfsX24) showed clinical features distinct from typical TKS (<citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31601675" doi="10.1084/jem.20190147" pmcid="PMC6888978" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32424669" doi="10.1007/s10875-020-00786-7" count="1">15</citation>, <citation rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31271789" doi="10.1016/j.jaci.2019.06.017" pmcid="PMC8425770" count="1">16</citation>). <sentence_start/>This condition is characterized by neonatal onset of pancytopenia, autoinflammation, rash, and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) (NOCARH syndrome). <sentence_start/>Since actin-based structures undergo continuous turnover regulated by CDC42 activity, mutants with impaired GDP/GTP regulation, such as constitutively active and loss-of-function variants, are thought to underlie CDC42-related disorders (<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21115489" doi="10.1074/jbc.R110.200329" pmcid="PMC3024731" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29394990" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.12.015" pmcid="PMC5985417" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although the Y64C mutant has been suggested to be constitutively active (<citation rid="bib17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32819561" doi="10.1016/j.bbrc.2020.06.104" count="1">17</citation>), the functional status of CDC42 mutants in TKS, especially their effects on the hearing phenotype, remains unclear.

In the present study, we examined Group I CDC42 mutants associated with classical TKS and investigated the relationship between CDC42 status and SNHL in a new patient with p.R68Q as well as reevaluation of Japanese patients carrying p.Y64C. We propose that CDC42 with impaired conversion between the GDP/inactive and GTP/active forms, including loss-of-function (<italic toggle="yes">i</italic>.<italic toggle="yes">e</italic>., <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO) and constitutively active mutants (<italic toggle="yes">i</italic>.<italic toggle="yes">e</italic>. Y64C and R68Q), likely causes SNHL in TKS. <sentence_start/>Moreover, we generated <italic toggle="yes">At</italic><italic toggle="yes">oh</italic><italic toggle="yes">1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup> (HC-specific <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-double KO [DKO]) mice to examine functional redundancy in hearing and demonstrated that CDC42 and RHOQ function synergistically in cochlear HCs.
Results
A patient with TKS possessing CDC42(R68Q) mutation

A 2-year-old Japanese female was referred to our hospital for hearing loss (HL). <sentence_start/>The mother’s pregnancy and delivery at 38 weeks of gestation were uneventful, and no family history of HL was reported. <sentence_start/>Profound bilateral HL was confirmed based on auditory brainstem response (ABR) at 3 months of age (Fig. S1<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>) and pure-tone audiometry at 4 years of age (Fig. S1<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>). <sentence_start/>High-resolution temporal bone computed tomography revealed no inner or middle ear anomalies (Fig. S1<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>). <sentence_start/>The patient had been using hearing aids in both ears since 1.5 years of age. <sentence_start/>Examination revealed dysmorphic facial features, intellectual disability, camptodactyly, cardiac anomalies (double-outlet right ventricle), and congenital hypothyroidism. <sentence_start/>Whole-exome sequencing demonstrated a <italic toggle="yes">CDC42</italic> variant ( , exon4:c.G203A: p.R68Q), which was present in the patient but not in the parents and was confirmed by direct sequence analysis (Fig. S1<italic toggle="yes">D</italic>). <sentence_start/>The patient was diagnosed with TKS based on the clinical and genetic findings. <sentence_start/>No family history of TKS was observed. <sentence_start/>May-Grünwald-Giemsa-stained blood smears confirmed macrothrombocytopenia. <sentence_start/>The patient had a history of recurrent acute otitis media in both ears. <sentence_start/>Patient information (Patient 4) and patients with TKS reported in Japan (re-evaluated in the present study, Patients 1-3) are summarized in Table 1.
Phenotypic properties of CDC42 mutants in cells

As an initial step, we examined the activity status of Group I TKS-associated CDC42 mutants-CDC42(Y64C), CDC42(R66G), and CDC42(R68Q)-in comparison with CDC42(WT) in HeLa cells, which served as a model system for investigating actin cytoskeletal structures, such as microvilli and stress fibers (<citation rid="bib18" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10559899" doi="10.1038/11056" count="1">18</citation>, <citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27707755" doi="10.15252/emmm.201606609" pmcid="PMC5090661" count="1">19</citation>, <citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31473629" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2019-106282" count="1">20</citation>). <sentence_start/>Stereocilia are an exquisitely organized subtype, with a tightly regulated length and shape, of microvilli and filopodia (<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27707755" doi="10.15252/emmm.201606609" pmcid="PMC5090661" count="1">19</citation>, <citation rid="bib21" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39843411" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-55898-8" pmcid="PMC11754657" count="1">21</citation>), and we previously reported CDC42-dependent developmental and morphological regulation of microvilli and stereocilia (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although cells expressing EGFP-CDC42(WT) or EGFP-CDC42(R66G) showed no enhanced staining of phalloidin compared with the surrounding non-transfected cells (Fig. 1, Movies S1-S4), those expressing EGFP-CDC42(Y64C) and EGFP-CDC42(R68Q) showed markedly enhanced dot-like phalloidin staining, indicating the presence of microvilli on the apical surface (Fig. 1, Movies S2 and S4). <sentence_start/>To determine whether cells expressing EGFP-CDC42 mutants exhibited actin accumulation compared with the surrounding non-expressing cells, the fluorescence intensity profiles across the yellow arrow for green (EGFP) and red (phalloidin) channels were analyzed using Zen software and plotted (Fig. 1, far right). <sentence_start/>Cells expressing CDC42(Y64C) or EGFP-CDC42(R68Q) showed higher phalloidin fluorescence intensity than the surrounding EGFP-negative cells, and EGFP and phalloidin signals colocalized at microvilli. <sentence_start/>In contrast, cells expressing EGFP-CDC42(WT) or EGFP-CDC42(R66G) did not show an apparent increase in phalloidin intensity compared with the surrounding EGFP-negative cells. <sentence_start/>Supporting these observations, a pulldown assay detecting GTP-bound (active) CDC42 showed that EGFP-tagged CDC42(Y64C), CDC42(R66G), and CDC42(R68Q) retained the active conformation more than EGFP-CDC42(WT) (Fig. S2). <sentence_start/>These results suggested that at least CDC42(Y64C) and CDC42(R68Q) are active mutants for microvilli.<sentence_start/>Figure 1

Marked rescue of the tight junction phenotype in MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup> cells by CDC42(Y64C) and CDC42(R68Q)

The CDC42 GEF Tuba localizes to tight junctions (TJs) through its interaction with ZO-1, and it stimulates CDC42-Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASP)-driven actin polymerization (<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17015620" doi="10.1083/jcb.200605012" pmcid="PMC2064505" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25469537" doi="10.4161/21541248.2014.973768" pmcid="PMC4601375" count="1">23</citation>). <sentence_start/>We previously reported that MDCK cells with stable <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> knockdown (MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup>) show disrupted ZO-1 staining (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>To further examine CDC42 mutant function, we established MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup> cells stably expressing EGFP-tagged CDC42(WT), CDC42(Y23C), Cdc42(Y64C), CDC42(R66G), or CDC42(R68Q) following doxycycline induction (Fig. 2, <italic toggle="yes">A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">B</italic>). <sentence_start/>Expression of all CDC42 variants significantly affected ZO-1 staining, and CDC42(Y64C)- or CDC42(R68Q)-expressing cells showed strong rescue of ZO-1 localization compared with uninduced cells (Fig. 2, <italic toggle="yes">A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">C</italic>). <sentence_start/>The difference between WT and CDC42(Y23C) showed a trend (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0697), whereas the difference between WT and CDC42(R66G) was significant (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0409; Fig. 2, <italic toggle="yes">A</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">C</italic>). <sentence_start/>These results suggest that CDC42(Y64C) and CDC42(R68Q) are strongly active mutants, while CDC42(Y23C) and CDC42(R66G) are weaker active mutants relative to CDC42(WT).Figure 2

Additional RhoQ deletion exacerbates hearing phenotypes in Cdc42-KO mice

We next examined functional redundancy between CDC42 and RHOQ. <sentence_start/>Reanalysis of our previous DNA microarray data from the whole cochlea of WT mice showed <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> expression ratios of 16847.4/64534.1 (1/3.83) at P6 and 5869.2/6740.6 (1/1.15) at P15 (<citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2023.106280" pmid="37666363" count="1">24</citation>). <sentence_start/>In contrast, cell type-specific RNA-sequencing analysis by Scheffer <italic toggle="yes">et al.</italic> (<citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25904789" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.5126-14.2015" pmcid="PMC4405555" count="1">5</citation>) showed expression ratios of approximately 1/4 to 5 at E16-P7 in cochlear HCs, with mRNA expression of <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> peaking at P0 and P4, respectively. <sentence_start/>ABR evaluation revealed normal hearing function in <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-KO mice at 6 and 8 weeks of age compared with control mice (Fig. 3<italic toggle="yes">A</italic>). <sentence_start/>In contrast, <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice (<italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>) showed more severe hearing impairment compared with <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice at 3 weeks of age, especially at low frequencies (click and 8 kHz) (Fig. 3<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>). <sentence_start/>The significance was highest at 3 weeks of age, gradually decreased, and was absent at 6 weeks (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0515 at click) (Fig. 3<italic toggle="yes">B</italic>). <sentence_start/>To explore the cause of this phenomenon (<italic toggle="yes">i</italic>.<italic toggle="yes">e</italic>., the significant difference observed at 3 weeks but not at 6 weeks), we examined mouse survival. <sentence_start/>By P60, 12 of 18 <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice had died, whereas only one <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mouse and no <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-KO mice had died (Fig. 3<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>). <sentence_start/>Because deaths were clustered during two periods (P15-P30 and P50-P60, Fig. 3<italic toggle="yes">C</italic>), we performed a more detailed survival analysis up to P30. <sentence_start/>By P30, 26 of 50 <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice had died, whereas no deaths were observed in either the <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO or <italic Discussion

CDC42, RHOQ, and RHOJ belong to the same subgroup of Rho-family small GTPases. <sentence_start/>RHOQ shares approximately 67% aa similarity with CDC42 in humans and mice, and is its closest homolog (<citation rid="bib36" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24297911" doi="10.1073/pnas.1309078110" pmcid="PMC3870750" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="bib37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnsyn.2022.959875" pmcid="PMC9386560" pmid="35989712" count="1">37</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although CDC42 has been extensively studied, RHOQ and RHOJ remain relatively understudied. <sentence_start/>RHOQ is involved in actin nucleation, particularly axon outgrowth (<citation rid="bib38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33156548" doi="10.1111/jnc.15235" count="1">38</citation>), and acts synergistically with CDC42 in Toll-like receptor signaling in B-cells (<citation rid="bib39" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28747344" doi="10.4049/jimmunol.1602167" pmcid="PMC5563166" count="1">39</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although RHOQ shows functional similarities to CDC42, it also has distinct roles and signaling pathways (<citation rid="bib40" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9799731" doi="10.1016/s0960-9822(07)00486-1" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="bib41" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11306516" count="1">41</citation>). <sentence_start/>CDC42 and RHOQ interact differently with the downstream protein collybistin (<citation rid="bib37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnsyn.2022.959875" pmcid="PMC9386560" pmid="35989712" count="1">37</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the present study, although RHOQ alone did not rescue TJ formation in MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup> cells, <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-KD impaired TJ formation. <sentence_start/>Moreover, additional deletion of <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> in <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice exacerbated hearing phenotypes in <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice. <sentence_start/>CDC42 is a known regulator of AJCs (<citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25469537" doi="10.4161/21541248.2014.973768" pmcid="PMC4601375" count="1">23</citation>); however, RHOQ involvement in AJCs has not previously been reported.

We previously reported that HC-specific <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice showed no PCP abnormalities in the cochlea (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>), consistent with another report (<citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fcell.2021.765559" pmcid="PMC8570139" pmid="34746154" count="1">25</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice exhibited a significantly increased number of fourth-row OHCs. <sentence_start/>Because PCP abnormalities occur in mice lacking <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> in both HCs and supporting cells (<citation rid="bib42" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25770185" doi="10.1242/bio.20149753" pmcid="PMC4400594" count="1">42</citation>), cochlear PCP may depend on CDC42-RHOQ signaling between these cell types. <sentence_start/>The mild PCP impairment without hair bundle disorientation observed in <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice may result from impaired AJC formation only in HCs. <sentence_start/>These mice also showed greater OHC loss at P18 than <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice, although OHC loss did not correlate with fourth-row OHC numbers at high frequencies, suggesting that the extra row does not directly cause OHC loss.

The more severe SNHL in <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice compared with <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice, particularly at low frequencies, gradually diminished and disappeared by 6 weeks of age, likely because severely affected mice died earlier. <sentence_start/>Although the exact mechanism of the earlier deaths is unclear, <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>, whose promoter was used to delete <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> in our mouse line, is also expressed in the brainstem, especially in respiratory nuclei, and conventional <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-KO mice exhibit perinatal lethality (<citation rid="bib43" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10364557" doi="10.1126/science.284.5421.1837" count="1">43</citation>, <citation rid="bib44" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19914183" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2009.10.023" pmcid="PMC2818435" count="1">44</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus, the earlier death of <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice may reflect synergistic roles of CDC42 and RHOQ in essential physiological processes.

patients with C81Y/F, one patient with S83P, and one patient with A159V (<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29394990" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.12.015" pmcid="PMC5985417" 1 (<citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31601675" doi="10.1084/jem.20190147" pmcid="PMC6888978" count="1">13</citation>), leaving the brain-dominant isoform 2 intact and producing milder actinopathies. <sentence_start/>Thus, SNHL appears characteristic of Group I TKS but uncommon in other CDC42-related disorders.

Our cell-based data demonstrated that Y64C and R68Q are active CDC42 mutants in terms of microvilli and TJ formation. <sentence_start/>In pulldown assays, Y64C, R66G, and R68Q mutants exhibited a greater tendency to maintain the active conformation than WT, with the R68Q mutant being the most active. <sentence_start/>The switch II region of CDC42 is critical for interaction with GDIs, GEFs, and GAPs (<citation rid="bib54" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15577926" doi="10.1038/sj.embor.7400293" pmcid="PMC1299188" count="1">54</citation>). <sentence_start/>Consistent with the results, the Y64C and R68Q mutants robustly impaired p50GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis (Y64C are 12-fold more insensitive to GAP than R68Q), whereas the R66G and Y23C mutants mildly impaired p50GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis (<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29394990" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.12.015" pmcid="PMC5985417" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, the Y64C mutant almost completely abolished the response to GEF, ITSN1, whereas the R68Q mutant slightly increased sensitivity (<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29394990" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.12.015" pmcid="PMC5985417" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>Taken together, Y64C and R68Q mutants are constitutively active, but the Y64C mutant may be a milder activating mutant than R68Q, rendering the Y64C mutant to be a more suitable active mutant in HeLa and MDCK cells, although both are harmful during development of the human cochlea. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, the Y64, R66, and R68 (<citation rid="bib55" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10676816" doi="10.1016/s0092-8674(00)80670-4" count="1">55</citation>, <citation rid="bib56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41589-025-02010-2" pmid="40846997" count="1">56</citation>) residues (although R68 to a lesser extent (<citation rid="bib54" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15577926" doi="10.1038/sj.embor.7400293" pmcid="PMC1299188" count="1">54</citation>, <citation rid="bib57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms222212493" pmcid="PMC8622166" pmid="34830380" count="1">57</citation>)) are critical for interactions with RhoGDI. <sentence_start/>Although the activity of the R66G and Y23C mutants was not as strong as that of the Y64C and R68Q mutants in the present study, the R66G and Y23C mutants lost their binding affinity to various effectors, including formin-like 2 (FMNL2) and IQ motif containing GTPase-activating protein 1 (IQGAP) (R66G) and p21-activated kinase 1 (PAK1), WASP, and FMNL2 (Y23C) (<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29394990" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.12.015" pmcid="PMC5985417" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus, the order of constitutive activity of CDC42 mutants may be influenced and determined by various conditions and timing of their existence and function, such as <italic toggle="yes">in vitro</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">in vivo</italic> settings and types of cell/organ/tissue. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, all patients with Y64C, R68Q, and Y23C mutations manifesting SNHL (<citation rid="bib50" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39755496" doi="10.1016/j.pedneo.2024.11.002" count="1">50</citation>, <citation rid="bib58" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31953712" doi="10.1007/s10875-020-00742-5" count="1">58</citation>, <citation rid="bib59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fgene.2023.1108852" pmcid="PMC10280004" pmid="37347054" count="1">59</citation>) simultaneously showed macrothrombocytopenia (MTC); however, MTC is not mentioned in patients with the R66G mutation (<citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29394990" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.12.015" pmcid="PMC5985417" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>MTC accompanied by hearing impairment has also been observed in <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="bib60" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20139097" doi="10.1182/blood-2009-09-242271" count="1">60</citation>), which show activated RhoA signaling with increased phospho-cofilin levels (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>); <italic toggle="yes">cofilin</italic>-KO mice (<citation rid="bib61" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20530287" doi="10.1182/blood-2010-03-274340" count="1">61</citation>, <citation rid="bib62" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29913074" doi="10.1080/09537104.2018.1478071" count="1">62</citation>, <citation rid="bib63" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39305224" doi="10.1002/cm.21933" pmcid="PMC11925801" count="1">63</citation>); patients with DFNA1 (deafness, non-syndromic, autosomal dominant 1) (<citation rid="bib64" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26912466" doi="10.1182/blood-2015-10-675629" count="1">64</citation>) and its model mice (<citation rid="bib65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202402118R" pmid="39831886" count="1">65</citation>) caused by constitutively active mutants of DIAPH1 (<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27707755" doi="10.15252/emmm.201606609" pmcid="PMC5090661" count="1">19</citation>, <citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31473629" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2019-106282" count="1">20</citation>, <citation rid="bib66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32678080" doi="10.1038/s41419-020-02743-z" pmcid="PMC7366933" count="1">66</citation>), a downstream molecule of RhoA; and <italic toggle="yes">RhoA</italic>-KO mice (<citation rid="bib67" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22045984" doi="10.1182/blood-2011-08-372193" count="1">67</citation>, <citation rid="bib68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1523/ENEURO.0149-17.2017" pmcid="PMC5602105" pmid="28929130" count="1">68</citation>). <sentence_start/>Together, these observations suggest that impaired regulation of RHOA signaling may lead to both MTC and SNHL.

Mice lacking cofilin and actin-depolymerizing factor (ADF) show abnormal cuticular plates and AJCs in cochlear HCs, leading to an abnormal stereocilia bundle shape and patterning (<citation rid="bib63" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39305224" doi="10.1002/cm.21933" pmcid="PMC11925801" count="1">63</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, imbalanced actin turnover caused by cofilin and ADF activity impedes TJ integrity in intestinal epithelial cells (<citation rid="bib69" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26878213" doi="10.1016/j.ajpath.2015.11.023" pmcid="PMC5807957" count="1">69</citation>, <citation rid="bib70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31849705" doi="10.3389/fphys.2019.01455" pmcid="PMC6901426" count="1">70</citation>). <sentence_start/>We previously showed that stable <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KD in MDCK cells enhances phospho-cofilin levels through the activated RhoA-ROCK-LIMK pathway, consistent with a report (<citation rid="bib71" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18045906" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3322-07.2007" pmcid="PMC6673401" count="1">71</citation>), leading to disrupted AJCs in cochlear HCs (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the present study, double KD of <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> synergistically enhanced phospho-cofilin levels in MDCK cells, suggesting their combined involvement in actin turnover. <sentence_start/>Elevated phospho-cofilin may therefore contribute to the more severe hearing phenotype of <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice compared with <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice at least through AJC disruption.

In conclusion, CDC42 and RHOQ function synergistically to establish and maintain cochlear HC integrity. <sentence_start/>CDC42 mutants that disrupt GTP/GDP cycling likely contribute to SNHL, particularly in Group I TKS. <sentence_start/>Because patients with the Y64C mutation show craniofacial malformations and brain anomalies (<citation rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26386261" doi="10.1002/ajmg.a.37275" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="bib47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejmg.2021.104358" pmid="34624555" count="1">47</citation>, <citation rid="bib58" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31953712" doi="10.1007/s10875-020-00742-5" count="1">58</citation>, <citation rid="bib72" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29335451" doi="10.1038/s10038-017-0396-5" count="1">72</citation>), including internal auditory canal stenosis and cochlear nerve hypoplasia (see Fig. S4 of Patient 3), and recurrent infections (<citation rid="bib58" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31953712" doi="10.1007/s10875-020-00742-5" count="1">58</citation>, <citation rid="bib59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fgene.2023.1108852" pmcid="PMC10280004" pmid="37347054" count="1">59</citation>, <citation rid="bib72" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29335451" doi="10.1038/s10038-017-0396-5" count="1">72</citation>), attention is required when diagnosing HL in TKS, because of congenital malformations in the cochlea and cochlear nerve, as well as ear infections (conductive HL). <sentence_start/>Indeed, Patient 4 in the present study and the patient with the C81Y mutation reported previously both manifested bilateral otitis media (<citation rid="bib49" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32231661" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2020.00318" pmcid="PMC7082228" count="1">49</citation>). <sentence_start/>Additionally, thyroid hormone is a critical factor for OHC maturation (<citation rid="bib73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2025.116898" pmid="41579371" count="1">73</citation>); thus, hypothyroidism, a representative symptom of Group I TKS (<citation rid="bib46" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30872706" doi="10.1038/s41598-019-40988-7" pmcid="PMC6418278" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="bib47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejmg.2021.104358" pmid="34624555" count="1">47</citation>, <citation rid="bib58" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31953712" doi="10.1007/s10875-020-00742-5" count="1">58</citation>, <citation rid="bib72" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29335451" doi="10.1038/s10038-017-0396-5" count="1">72</citation>), should also be considered during follow-up of SNHL in TKS (Patients 3 (<citation rid="bib72" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29335451" doi="10.1038/s10038-017-0396-5" count="1">72</citation>), and 4). <sentence_start/>Further studies using longitudinal patient data are required to better understand the relationship between CDC42 functional status and hearing phenotypes in TKS, as well as the natural history of SNHL in TKS associated with hypothyroidism.
Experimental procedures
Ethics approval and consent to participate

This study was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of Kobe University (references 26-03-05, 2020-06-04, and 2024-03-03) and conducted in accordance with the Animal Experimentation Regulations of Kobe University. <sentence_start/>The human study was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of the Ryukyus (registration number: 20-271-04-00-01) and the ethics committee of Keio University School of Medicine (approval number: 20110262), and performed in accordance with the ethical standards stated in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki. <sentence_start/>Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before inclusion in the study.
Generation of Atoh1-Cre;Cdc42<sup>flox/flox</sup>;RhoQ<sup>flox/flox</sup> (Cdc42;RhoQ-DKO) mice

We deleted <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> from inner ear HCs of <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic> transgenic mice (<citation rid="bib74" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16145671" doi="10.1002/dvdy.20551" pmcid="PMC1343505" count="1">74</citation>, <citation rid="bib75" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22526732" doi="10.1007/s10162-012-0324-5" pmcid="PMC3346893" count="1">75</citation>, <citation rid="bib76" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37204479" doi="10.1007/s00109-023-02317-4" pmcid="PMC10300165" count="1">76</citation>). <sentence_start/>HC-specific <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO mice, <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup> (<italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>−/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup> as controls), have been reported previously (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/+</sup> mice (<citation rid="bib39" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28747344" doi="10.4049/jimmunol.1602167" pmcid="PMC5563166" count="1">39</citation>) (RRID:IMSR_JAX:030928) were purchased from Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup> and <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/+</sup> mice were backcrossed to generate <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/+</sup> and <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>−/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/+</sup> mice and then crossed to obtain <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup>+/+</sup> (<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO) and <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>+/−</sup>;<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><sup><italic toggle="yes">flox</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">flox</italic></sup> (<italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO). <sentence_start/>Age- and sex-matched siblings of the <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic><sup>−/−</sup> genotype obtained by crossing were used as controls.

Offspring were genotyped <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using the following primer pairs: <italic toggle="yes">Atoh1</italic>-<italic toggle="yes">Cre</italic> (5′-GCATACCTGGAAAATGCTTC-3′ and 5′-CCAGTGAAACAGCATTGCTG-3′; yielding 250-bp product), <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>flox</sup></italic> (5′-ATCGGTCACTGTTCTACTTTG-3′ and 5′-TACTGCTATGACTGAAAACCTC-3′; yielding 162-bp product), <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>flox</sup></italic> (5′-CAGGGGCCACATTACACCT-3′ and 5′-GTGGGGAGAGAAGCTCACAG-3′; yielding 219-bp product).

Mice were group-housed in the animal facility of Kobe University under specific pathogen-free conditions using an individually ventilated care system (Tecniplast Japan) and were maintained on a 14 h light and 10 h dark cycle at 23 °C ± 2 deg and 50 ± 10% humidity, with food and water provided <italic toggle="yes">ad libitum</italic>. <sentence_start/>All mice were identified using numbered ear tags. <sentence_start/>Both male and female mice were used in the analyses unless otherwise indicated (mice < 3 weeks of age were not differentiated based on sex).
Antibodies

The following antibodies were used: rabbit anti-CDC42 (Cell Signaling Technology [CST], Danvers, MA, USA; Cat# 2462, RRID: ); rabbit anti-RHOQ (Proteintech, Cat# 17805-1-AP, RRID: ); rabbit anti-phospho-cofilin (Ser3) (77G2) (CST; Cat#3313, RRID: ); rabbit anti-ZO-1 (Proteintech; Cat# 21773-1-AP, RRID: ); rabbit anti-vinculin (Proteintech, Cat# 26520-1-AP, RRID: ); rabbit anti-calnexin (Abcam; Cat# ab22595, RRID: ), mouse anti-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) conjugated with HRP and rabbit anti-α-tubulin conjugated with HRP (MBL, Tokyo, Japan; Cat# M171-7, RRID: and Cat# PM054-7, RRID: , respectively). <sentence_start/>Validation data for each antibody were obtained from the respective companies.
Auditory brainstem response (ABR) measurements

Hearing was assessed <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> ABR measurements at the indicated ages in <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-KO, <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>-KO, and <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>;<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic>-DKO mice and littermate control mice, as described previously (<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27707755" doi="10.15252/emmm.201606609" pmcid="PMC5090661" count="1">19</citation>). <sentence_start/>Briefly, mice were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of an anesthetic cocktail (medetomidine 0.3 mg/kg, midazolam 4.0 mg/kg, and butorphanol 5.0 mg/kg) and placed on a heating pad to maintain body temperature. <sentence_start/>BioSigRP Software and TDT System 3 (Tucker-Davis Technologies, Alachua, FL, USA) were used to generate all stimuli and record responses. <sentence_start/>The ABR waveforms were recorded for 12.8 ms at a sampling rate of 40,000 Hz using a 50 to 5000 Hz passband, and 500 responses were averaged for each sound pressure level (SPL). <sentence_start/>Clicks and 8-32-kHz tone bursts were presented in 5 dB steps from 90 dB SPL below the threshold to up to 10 dB SPL. <sentence_start/>Hearing threshold was defined as the lowest sound intensity level at which a recognizable or reproducible wave III was observed. <sentence_start/>When no response to stimulation at 90 dB was observed, the threshold was set to 100 dB.
Plasmids

Short hairpin RNA for canine <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> (nucleotides 197-215 from <italic toggle="yes">ATG</italic> [<italic toggle="yes">sh197</italic>])-resistant human <italic toggle="yes">CDC42</italic> in pEGFP(C1) (Takara Bio, Kusatsu, Japan) has been reported (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>Human <italic toggle="yes">RHOQ</italic> in pEGFP(C1) was prepared by PCR using human <italic toggle="yes">RHOQ</italic> in pCMV-SPORT6 (provided by RIKEN BRC through the National BioResource Project of MEXT, Japan) and an In-Fusion HD cloning kit (Takara Bio) (<citation rid="bib77" ref-type="bibr" pmid="14702039" doi="10.1038/ng1285" count="1">77</citation>). <sentence_start/>All mutations (Y23C, Y64C, R66G, and R68Q in <italic toggle="yes">CDC42</italic>; Q67L and Y70C in <italic toggle="yes">RHOQ</italic>, corresponding to Q61L, a constitutively active mutant (<citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33347888" doi="10.1016/j.bpj.2020.12.007" pmcid="PMC7840443" count="1">10</citation>), and Y64C in CDC42) were introduced using the QuickChange Lightning Site-Directed Mutagenesis kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), and named EGFP-CDC42(Y23C), EGFP-CDC42(Y64C), EGFP-CDC42(R66G), EGFP-CDC42(R68Q), EGFP-RHOQ(Q67L), and EGFP-RHOQ(Y70C).

The doxycycline-inducible vector, pRetroX-TetOne-Puro, was purchased from Takara Bio. <italic toggle="yes">sh</italic><italic toggle="yes">197</italic>-resistant EGFP-CDC42(WT), EGFP-CDC42(Y23C), EGFP-CDC42(Y64C), EGFP-CDC42(R66G), and EGFP-CDC42(R68Q), and EGFP-RHOQ(WT), EGFP-RHOQ(Q67L), and EGFP-RHOQ(Y70C) were amplified by PCR and cloned into the EcoRI/BamHI sites of the vector using an In-Fusion HD cloning kit. <sentence_start/>These constructs were named tetEGFP-CDC42(WT), tetEGFP-CDC42(Y23C), tetEGFP-CDC42(Y64C), tetEGFP-CDC42(R66G), tetEGFP-CDC42(R68Q), tetEGFP-RHOQ (WT), tetEGFP-RHOQ (Q67L), and tetEGFP-RHOQ(Y70C).
Cells

HeLa (<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27707755" doi="10.15252/emmm.201606609" pmcid="PMC5090661" count="1">19</citation>), MDCK (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>), and MDCK cells stably expressing <italic toggle="yes">sh197</italic> (targeting <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic>) in <italic toggle="yes">pSUPER</italic>(<italic toggle="yes">neo</italic>) (MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup>) (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>) have been previously described. <sentence_start/>MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup> cells were cultured with 300 μg/ml G418. <sentence_start/>To establish MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup> with stable tetEGFP-CDC42(WT), tetEGFP-CDC42(Y23C), tetEGFP-CDC42(Y64C), tetEGFP-CDC42(R66G), tetEGFP-CDC42(R68Q), tetEGFP-RHOQ(WT), tetEGFP-RHOQ(Q67L), or tetEGFP-RHOQ(Y70C) expression, MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup> were electroporated using a NEPA21 electroporator (NEPA GENE, Ichikawa, Japan), and then selected using 300 μg/ml G418 and 5 μg/ml puromycin (FUJIFILM). <sentence_start/>Clone establishment was confirmed by immunoblotting with antibodies against CDC42 and RHOQ. <sentence_start/>Cells were maintained in D-MEM (FUJIFILM) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Nichirei Biosciences), 100 units/ml penicillin, and 100 μg/ml streptomycin in a 5% CO<sub>2</sub> humidified incubator at 37 °C.
Immunoblotting

Cells were lysed by sonication in homogenizing buffer (<citation rid="bib78" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11723183" doi="10.1046/j.1471-4159.2001.00624.x" count="1">78</citation>) containing a Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Nacalai Tesque). <sentence_start/>Total cell lysates were centrifuged at 900<italic toggle="yes">g</italic> for 5 min at 4 °C, and the supernatants were subjected to sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) followed by blocking with 1% fat-free bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 1 h at 23 °C and immunoblotting for 2 h at 23 °C using primary antibodies diluted in tris-buffered saline (TBS) containing 0.03% Triton X-100 (TX). <sentence_start/>Bound primary antibodies were detected with secondary antibody-horseradish peroxidase (HRP) conjugates using an enhanced chemiluminescence detection system (Clarity; Bio-Rad Laboratories) and FUSION SOLO S with Evolution Capt software (Vilber). <sentence_start/>For quantification, the relative expression levels of phospho-cofilin were normalized to those of vinculin or calnexin.
Confocal imaging

To analyze the surface preparation of the organ of Corti, anesthetized mice were transcardially fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) (<citation rid="bib78" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11723183" doi="10.1046/j.1471-4159.2001.00624.x" count="1">78</citation>). <sentence_start/>The dissected inner ears were decalcified in 0.12 M ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) for 2 days at 23 °C (<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27707755" doi="10.15252/emmm.201606609" pmcid="PMC5090661" count="1">19</citation>) and then further dissected into apical, middle, and basal turn pieces. <sentence_start/>Tissues were permeabilized with 0.3% TX, blocked with 5% fat-free BSA, and incubated with Alexa Fluor 488-labeled phalloidin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# A12381; 1:750) and 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) in TBS containing 0.03% TX for 2 h at 23 °C. <sentence_start/>The tissues were then rinsed in TBS containing 0.03% TX and mounted on coverslips using ProLong Antifade (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

To examine the rescue effect of CDC42 and RHOQ on TJ formation using MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup> cells stably expressing doxycycline-inducible plasmids, the cells were incubated with 100 ng/ml doxycycline 8 h after seeding on a 35-mm glass-bottom dish (Mattek, Ashland, MA, USA). <sentence_start/>Forty-eight hours after incubation, the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.3% TX, stained with ZO-1 antibody for 2 h at 23 °C, followed by incubation with Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated secondary antibodies and DAPI for 0.5 h at 23 °C.

Imaging was performed using a confocal microscope (LSM900; Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany) with a 40× or 63× oil immersion objective. <sentence_start/>Orthogonal projection images were generated from each z-stack image using ZEN software (Carl Zeiss). <sentence_start/>The fluorescence intensity profiles across the arrow for green and red channels were analyzed using Zen software and are shown in the graphs. <sentence_start/>To evaluate ZO-1 staining in MDCK<sup>Cdc42KD</sup> cells (rescue experiments), the number of cells with ZO-1 staining in more than half of their perimeter was counted, and the percentage (divided by the total cell number identified by DAPI) was calculated. <sentence_start/>To evaluate ZO-1 staining in WT MDCK cells (KD experiments), the number of cells whose contours were identified by ZO-1 staining was counted, and the percentage (cells with contours of ZO-1 staining) was calculated.
Pulldown assay for CDC42 activation

Pulldown assay was performed using a Rac1/Cdc42 Activation Magnetic Beads Pulldown Assay kit (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. <sentence_start/>Briefly, EGFP-CDC42(WT), EGFP-CDC42(Y64C), EGFP-CDC42(R66G), or EGFP-CDC42(R68Q) were electroporated into 2.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> HeLa cells using a NEPA21 electroporator (NEPA GENE). <sentence_start/>Forty-eight hours after transfection, the cells were lysed in 400 μl of lysis buffer, and the total cell lysates were centrifuged at 14,000<italic toggle="yes">g</italic> for 5 min at 4 °C. <sentence_start/>After saving the aliquots (40 μl) for loading control, the residual supernatants were agitated without or with 100 μM GTPγS or 1mM GDP for 30 min at 30 °C. <sentence_start/>Then, the supernatants were rotated with magnetic beads conjugated with the p21-binding domain (PBD) of PAK1 for 45 min at 4 °C. <sentence_start/>The precipitates were washed three times using a magnetic rack, and the material absorbed to beads was eluted in Laemmli’s sample buffer. <sentence_start/>The aliquots of elutants were subjected to SDS-PAGE followed by immunoblotting using a CDC42 antibody. <sentence_start/>For quantification, the relative amounts of active EGFP-tagged CDC42 proteins were normalized to expression levels of each EGFP-tagged CDC42 protein.
Transient CDC42 and RHOQ knockdown

The RNAi sequence for canine and human <italic toggle="yes">Cdc42</italic> (siCdc42: 5′-GATTACGACCGCTGAGTTA-3′) has been previously described (<citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24610943" doi="10.1242/jcs.143602" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="bib79" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29253508" doi="10.1016/j.expneurol.2017.12.003" count="1">79</citation>). <sentence_start/>The siRNAs for canine <italic toggle="yes">RhoQ</italic> (si<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ-1</italic>: 5′-TGCACCAAATGTACCCTTT-3′; si<italic toggle="yes">RhoQ-2</italic>: 5′-CTGTCCATTTCTCTCAAAA-3′) and control were purchased from Nippon Gene. <sentence_start/>The siRNAs were transfected into MDCK cells using RNAiMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and used in the experiments 48 h later.
Human study

Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen). <sentence_start/>Whole-exome sequencing was performed using the SureSelect Human All Exon V6 kit (Agilent Technologies) for capture and HiSeq2500 (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) for sequencing with 101-bp paired-end reads. <sentence_start/>The total reads were aligned to GRCh37 using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner ( ). <sentence_start/>Variants were called using GATK Unified Genotyper and ANNOVAR ( ). <sentence_start/>Detected variants were validated by Sanger sequencing.
Quantification and statistical analysis
